project: What Does the Internet Know About You?
disclaimer: Fictional character and illustrative data traces. Research numbers apply only to specified study populations.

scenes.title: The Hook
scenes.narration: You're three years old. You tap a video on a parent's tablet. You can't even read yet. But your digital footprint may already be beginning.
scenes.onscreen: Your digital footprint may start before you can read.
scenes.visual: Fade from black to a child silhouette and an unbranded tablet. A single video card appears; one faint observation node glows. Do NOT label the child as identified by an ad network.

scenes.title: First Videos
scenes.narration: In 2026, Dutch children aged zero to six spent an average of 102 minutes a day looking at screens. Video viewing can leave traces.
scenes.visual: Animate a 102-minute counter next to a clearly labelled population chart. The number is the GROUP average, never a statistic about our specific 3-year-old. Reveal watch/search history as possible service-local signals.

scenes.title: First Smartphone
scenes.narration: At nine, our character gets a first phone. Dutch research puts the average at 9.2 years. With a personal device, online activity can become more independent.
scenes.onscreen: 9.2 years  ·  Average first phone age  ·  Netherlands
scenes.visual: Timeline moves to age nine. Tablet shrinks; the silhouette gains a phone. Add distinct app bubbles without brand logos. Label the phone statistic as parent-reported and not universal.

scenes.title: First Social Account
scenes.narration: At eleven comes a first social media account. In one Flemish study, the reported average was ten years and three months. Likes and follows add clues.
scenes.onscreen: 10 years, 3 months  ·  Parent-reported first account  ·  Flanders
scenes.visual: Animate a sample account card and likes/follows floating toward the user’s platform-local data cluster. Mark age eleven as FICTIONAL; 10y3m as the study mean for the eligible respondents.

scenes.title: Online Identity
scenes.narration: By fourteen, videos, messages and shared posts can reveal interests and social connections. Not every action is public, and not every service collects the same information.
scenes.onscreen: What you share  ≠  What a platform observes
scenes.visual: Split screen into voluntarily shared content versus observed interactions. Use privacy lock symbols for private messages; DO NOT display private message content as always accessible to advertisers. Visual is illustrative, not proof of how a named provider processes data.

scenes.title: Digital Consumer
scenes.narration: At eighteen, shopping, subscriptions and everyday apps add more kinds of data. In-game purchases often begin even earlier. But this isn't one giant profile shared by everyone.
scenes.onscreen: More services. More types of data. Not one universal database.
scenes.visual: Draw SEPARATE translucent containers for video, social, and shopping platforms with no default cross-platform arrows. Mention earlier game purchases as a caption; do not imply age 18 marks the first online purchase.

scenes.title: From Data to Prediction
scenes.narration: Here's the twist: data can become predictions. If someone watches running videos and searches for training tips, a platform might infer they're interested in running. That's a guess, not a fact.
scenes.onscreen: Observed signals → Possible inference: Interested in running
scenes.visual: Zoom into ONE hypothetical service. Three observed running-related actions converge toward a purple predicted-interest chip. Purple inference must be labelled “possible” and must not count as a proven personal fact.

scenes.title: The Feedback Loop
scenes.narration: That guess can influence recommendations. You watch, click, or scroll. Your response gives the system more signals. The loop keeps going.
scenes.visual: Show one loop: purple predicted interest → amber recommendation → cyan interaction → return to model. Never portray an algorithm as always perfectly predicting or manipulating actions.

scenes.title: The Open Ending
scenes.narration: So as these systems learn from your choices, how much might they shape what you choose next?
scenes.onscreen: How much might they shape your next choice?
scenes.visual: Fade the previous elements. Pause on the fictional profile silhouette and the open question. End with small “Research sources & methods” cue. Avoid dystopian certainty.
